raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old shepherd residing in a malaria-endemic area in Mauritania (Kobeni, Hodh El Gharbi) with no remarkable history of renal disease presented with fever associated with chills, myalgia, vomiting, and loss of consciousness on September 2, 2015. The patient developed a flu-like syndrome (fever, headache, and arthralgia) and abdominal pain 3 days before hospitalization in Aioun hospital (reference hospital of Hodh El Gharbi region). Clinical examination on admission showed severe impairment of consciousness with a Glasgow score of 8, jaundice, dyspnea, and pallor. He had no rashes, edema, or palpable lymph nodes. The patient had hypotension (60/40 mmHg), tachycardia, tachypnea (38 breaths/min), and hyperthermia (40.5 C). The rapid diagnostic test for malaria and microscopic examination of blood smears were positive for P. falciparum. Laboratory examinations showed the following results: hemoglobin, 7 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 87 fL; aspartate amino-transferase, 104 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase, 93 IU/L; total bilirubin, 49 mumol/L; direct bilirubin, 77 mumol/L; and random blood glucose, 1.02 g/L. Urinalysis and cerebrospinal fluid tests were negative.
On the second day of hospitalization, the patient developed shortness of breath with no cough and anuria (with only 50 mL urine collected over 24 hours); this was soon followed by hiccups. A chest X-ray was performed, which helped confirm a diagnosis of pulmonary edema. The renal workup revealed serum creatinine of 102 mg/dL, serum urea of 1.17 g/L (high), serum potassium of 5.1 mEq/L, and serum sodium of 142 mEq/L. On the basis of these results, the patient was diagnosed as having severe malaria with acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, and anemia. The patient was admitted to the hemodialysis unit for emergency dialysis. Quinine (10 mg/kg body weight) was administered every 8 hours in 5% dextrose infusion for 4 days. Volume expansion, antipyretic treatment, and diuretics were administered. After two sessions of consecutive hemodialysis of 4 h/d, the patient became conscious and had urine output of 1900 mL/24 h. Serum creatinine, urea, and potassium were 29 mg/dL, 0.47 g/L, and 4 mEq/L, respectively. The patient was discharged from the hospital 4 days later in good health. The follow-on oral treatment was a full course of artesunate-sulfamethoxypyrazine-pyrimethamine (Co-arinate FDC ; Dafra Pharma, Turnhout, Belgium) for 3 days. The patient was closely followed up after 3 weeks and was found to have normal and stable renal function, and he was also asymptomatic. Adjuvant therapy was prescribed, and no control blood smear for malaria parasites was made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presenting with a 3-day history of high fever of 40.5 C, chills, vomiting, abdominal pain, severe hypotension, and loss of consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 3 days prior to admission with a flu-like illness (fever, headache, arthralgia), abdominal pain, myalgia, and recurrent vomiting. On the day of admission, he suffered acute neurological decline with loss of consciousness and cardiovascular collapse. On hospital day 2, he developed acute dyspnea, hiccups, and profound anuria (24-hour urine output of only 50 mL), diagnosed with pulmonary edema and severe acute kidney injury requiring urgent hemodialysis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resides in a malaria-endemic area (Kobeni, Hodh El Gharbi, Mauritania) working as a shepherd. No prior history of renal disease, hypertension, or diabetes.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, myalgias, arthralgias, headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, dyspnea, hiccups, anuria, and coma. Negative for cough or rash. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 40.5 C, blood pressure: 60/40 mmHg (hypotension/shock), tachycardia, respiratory rate: 38 breaths/min (tachypnea). Neurological: Severe impairment of consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 8. General appearance: Marked pallor, jaundice, dyspnea in respiratory distress; no skin rashes, peripheral edema, or palpable lymphadenopathy. Follow-up exam on day 2 revealed pulmonary edema with tachypnea and persistent anuria.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 7 g/dL, MCV: 87 fL. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 104 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 93 IU/L, total bilirubin: 49 mumol/L, direct bilirubin: 77 mumol/L, random blood glucose: 1.02 g/L. Urinalysis: Negative. Day 2 renal panel: Serum creatinine: 102 mg/dL, serum urea: 1.17 g/L, serum potassium: 5.1 mEq/L, serum sodium: 142 mEq/L. Post-dialysis laboratory values: Serum creatinine: 29 mg/dL, serum urea: 0.47 g/L, serum potassium: 4 mEq/L. Chest radiograph: Confirmed acute pulmonary edema.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: Cytochemical tests within normal limits (negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe, life-threatening Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by septic/hypovolemic shock, cerebral malaria (GCS 8), severe acute kidney injury (anuria), non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hyperbilirubinemia, and severe anemia.
Diagnostic confirmation: Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and Giemsa-stained microscopic blood smears were positive for Plasmodium falciparum. Meningitis was excluded by normal CSF examination.
Plan & Outcome: Resuscitation with cautious intravenous volume expansion, antipyretics, loop diuretics, and emergent hemodialysis (two consecutive 4-hour daily sessions). Antimalarial therapy initiated with intravenous quinine (10 mg/kg body weight every 8 hours in 5% dextrose infusion for 4 days). Following dialysis, sensorium cleared completely, and brisk diuresis ensued (1,900 mL/24 h). Discharged on day 6 to complete a 3-day oral course of fixed-dose combination artesunate-sulfamethoxypyrazine-pyrimethamine (Co-arinate FDC). At 3-week follow-up, renal function was completely normal and stable, and the patient remained asymptomatic.
